# Lisp rules

## lisp-project

Project structure for Common Lisp on Allegro CL. Use when creating or changing a .asd system, a package.lisp, a project's file layout or dependencies, or a project's tester tests.

A Lisp project is one system definition (`NAME.asd`), one package file, the
source files and a tests file. Copy the shape of `examples/tally/`, which
loads through ASDF and passes `lisp-check`.

### Layout

```
tally/
  tally.asd          system definition
  package.lisp       defpackage, loaded first
  tally.lisp         source, starts with (in-package :tally)
  tally-tests.lisp   tester tests
```

A bigger project puts source in `src/` and tests in `tests/`, like
`examples/shapes/`; see `references/asdf.md`. Keep the `.asd` at the
project root.

### Packages

Define the package once, in `package.lisp`:

```lisp
(defpackage :tally
  (:use :cl)
  (:export #:split-words
           #:tally-words
           #:word-count
           #:top-words))
```

- Name symbols as `#:name` or `:name`, in lower case (case-mode rule below).
- `:use` only `:cl`, plus `:util.test` in a tests package. Refer to any other
  package's symbols with a prefix: `excl.osi:command-output`, `tally:tally-words`.
- `:export` every symbol other packages or the tests call.
- Every other source file starts with `(in-package :tally)` and defines no
  package of its own.
- A tests file defines its own package, named `NAME-tests`, that `:use`s the
  package under test.

### The system definition

From `examples/tally/tally.asd`:

```lisp
(asdf:defsystem "tally"
  :description "Count how often each word occurs in a text."
  :version "0.1.0"
  :serial t
  :components ((:file "package")
               (:file "tally"))
  :in-order-to ((test-op (load-op "tally/tests"))))

(asdf:defsystem "tally/tests"
  :depends-on ("tally" (:require "tester"))
  :components ((:file "tally-tests")))
```

- Name the file after the system: system `"tally"` lives in `tally.asd`.
  A second system in the same file is named `"tally/tests"`.
- `:serial t` loads the components in the order listed, so the order is the
  load order:
  1. `package` first, because every other file says `(in-package :tally)`.
  2. Then each file before the files that use its macros, variables or
     classes. A macro must be loaded before any file that calls it.
- `:file` takes the name without `.lisp`.
- When you add a source file, add it to `:components` in the right place.
  A file missing from the `.asd` is never loaded.
- The tests system is separate, so loading `"tally"` does not run the tests.

### Dependencies

There is no Quicklisp and no other package manager, and the machine may have
no network. A project uses only:

- Allegro's built-in modules, loaded with `require`. In a source file:
  `(eval-when (:compile-toplevel :load-toplevel :execute) (require :osi))`.
  In the `.asd`: `:depends-on ((:require "osi"))`.
- Other ASDF systems that already exist in the project or on the machine, by
  name in `:depends-on`.

When the code needs a library the project does not have (for example
`alexandria`, `cl-ppcre` or `split-sequence`), write the few functions it
needs in the project, or ask the user.

### Loading and testing

At the REPL, with the `.asd` file's absolute path:

```lisp repl
(require :asdf)
(asdf:load-asd #p"/path/to/tally/tally.asd")
(asdf:load-system "tally")
(asdf:test-system "tally")    ; loads "tally/tests", which runs the tests
```

`lisp-check` does the loading for you: when the file's directory or a parent
has `.asd` files, it loads those systems before compiling the file. So check
every project file on its own:

```sh
lisp-check tally/package.lisp
lisp-check tally/tally.lisp
lisp-check --test tally/tally-tests.lisp
```

A `system:` problem means the project failed to load. The message names the
`.asd` and usually the file that broke: run `lisp-check` on that file and fix
it first, or fix the `.asd`.

Some mistakes show only when the code loads, for example a `defmethod` whose
arguments do not match its `defgeneric`. After changing source, run the tests
file with `--test`.

### Tests

Write tests with Allegro's built-in `tester` module (package `util.test`),
in `NAME-tests.lisp`, as top-level `(test ...)` forms. The file format and the
rules are in the lisp-verify skill's `references/tester-tests.md`. Read it
before writing a tests file. A project tests file differs in one line: its
package also uses the package under test.

```lisp
(defpackage :tally-tests
  (:use :cl :util.test :tally))
```

### Case mode: alisp unless the project says otherwise

Assume `alisp`, Allegro's ANSI mode, which reads `foo` and `FOO` as the same
symbol. Switch to `mlisp` (case-sensitive) only when the project says so, for
example in its README or build scripts, or when the user does. Write all code
and all `defpackage` names in lower case so it works in both. The lisp-writing
skill has the details. (Allegro Express has no `mlisp`, so `mlisp` behaviour is
not verified here.)

### References

- `references/asdf.md`: `src/` and `tests/` modules, `:depends-on` between
  components, loading a project by hand, where ASDF puts compiled files.

### ASDF details

ASDF 3 ships with Allegro CL: `(require :asdf)`. This file covers what the
skill leaves out.

#### Source in `src/`, tests in `tests/`

`examples/shapes/` passes `lisp-check`:

```
shapes/
  shapes.asd
  src/package.lisp
  src/macros.lisp
  src/area.lisp
  src/report.lisp          uses excl.osi, from the built-in osi module
  tests/shapes-tests.lisp
```

```lisp
(asdf:defsystem "shapes"
  :depends-on ((:require "osi"))
  :components ((:module "src"
                :components ((:file "package")
                             (:file "macros" :depends-on ("package"))
                             (:file "area" :depends-on ("package" "macros"))
                             (:file "report" :depends-on ("area")))))
  :in-order-to ((test-op (load-op "shapes/tests"))))

(asdf:defsystem "shapes/tests"
  :depends-on ("shapes" (:require "tester"))
  :components ((:module "tests"
                :components ((:file "shapes-tests")))))
```

- `(:module "src" :components (...))` loads files from the `src/` directory.
- Order the components one of two ways:
  - `:serial t` on the system or module: each file depends on all files
    listed before it. Simple; use it for small projects.
  - `:depends-on ("file" ...)` on each component: names the files in the same
    module that must load first. The `package` file comes first in every
    chain, and a file that uses a macro depends on the file defining it.
- `:depends-on` on the system lists other systems and built-in modules:
  `"other-system"`, `(:require "osi")`, `(:require "tester")`.
- `lisp-check` finds `shapes.asd` from `src/` and `tests/` too: it looks in
  the file's directory, then each parent, up to the directory holding `.git`.

#### Loading a project by hand

```lisp repl
(require :asdf)
(asdf:load-asd #p"/path/to/shapes/shapes.asd")   ; absolute path
(asdf:load-system "shapes")
(asdf:test-system "shapes")
```

- `load-asd` tells ASDF about the systems in that file. Do it once per `.asd`
  before `load-system`.
- `load-system` compiles each file whose source changed, then loads it.
- `test-system` runs the system's `test-op`, which here loads
  `"shapes/tests"`. Loading the tests file runs its top-level assertions.
  Failures print `Test failed:` blocks; the counts are in
  `util.test:*test-errors*` and `util.test:*test-successes*`.

#### Where compiled files go

ASDF writes fasls to `~/.cache/common-lisp/<implementation>/`, under the
source file's absolute path, never next to the source. `lisp-check` sends
them to `/tmp/lisp-check-asdf/` instead. Keep `*.fasl` in `.gitignore` anyway.

#### Common mistakes

- A file that is not in `:components` is never loaded. Add every new file.
- The `package` file must load before any file that says `in-package`.
- The main system has a different name than its `.asd` file. `lisp-check`
  loads the system named like the file: `"shapes"` from `shapes.asd`.
- `:depends-on` names a system that is not on the machine, for example a
  Quicklisp library. Write the code in the project instead.

## lisp-verify

Check loop for Common Lisp. Use after writing or editing any Lisp source or test file (.lisp, .cl) to run lisp-check, fix the first error, and repeat until OK.

Every Lisp file you write must pass `lisp-check`. A file is done only when
`lisp-check` prints `OK` for it.

### The loop

For each Lisp file you created or changed:

1. Run `lisp-check path/to/file.lisp`. If the file has `tester` tests, run
   `lisp-check --test path/to/file.lisp` instead.
2. Read the output. The last line is `OK` or `FAIL`.
3. If the last line is `OK`, this file is done. Go to the next file.
4. If the last line is `FAIL`, fix **only the first problem line** in the output.
   Make the smallest edit that fixes it. Keep the rest of the file as it is.
5. Go back to step 1.

Fix one problem per round. Later problems are often caused by the first one,
so they may disappear once it is fixed.

Finish the loop before you report the work as done. When you report, say that
`lisp-check` printed `OK` for each file.

### When to use `--test`

`--test` also loads the compiled file, which runs its top-level `tester`
assertions (`(test ...)`, `(test-error ...)`).

- Use `--test` on every test file, usually named `NAME-tests.lisp`. To
  write one, see [references/tester-tests.md](references/tester-tests.md).
- Check other files without `--test`: a file with no assertions fails with
  `no tester assertions ran`.
- When you change code that a test file covers, run the loop on the test
  file with `--test` too.

### Reading the output

Each problem is one line:

```
FILE:LINE: STAGE: MESSAGE
```

- `LINE` is the line number to look at. `?` means the line is unknown.
- `STAGE` says which check found the problem.
- `MESSAGE` says what is wrong.

After the problem lines comes exactly one summary line: `OK` or `FAIL`.
The exit code is `0` for `OK`, `1` when the file has problems, and `2` when
`lisp-check` itself could not run.

#### Stage `read`

The file does not read as Lisp. Usually the parentheses or quotes do not
balance.

```
src/math.lisp:9: read: form starting here is never closed (missing ')', '"' or '|#')
FAIL
```

This means the top-level form that starts on line 9 is missing a closing
`)`, a closing `"` or a closing `|#`. The missing character belongs somewhere
inside that form, not at the end of the file. To fix it:

1. Go to the form that starts on that line.
2. Count `(` and `)` in that form, one inner form at a time.
3. Add the missing `)` where the inner form should end.
4. Check that every string `"` and every `#|` comment is closed.

```
src/math.lisp:7: read: Invalid unmatched right parenthesis read.
FAIL
```

Line 7 has one `)` too many. Remove the extra `)` on that line, or add the
`(` that is missing before it.

Other `read` messages name the bad syntax, for example
`Comma not inside a backquote.` Fix the syntax on that line.

#### Stage `system`

The file is in a project (a `.asd` in its directory or a parent), and
`lisp-check` could not load that ASDF system. Run `lisp-check` on the project
file the message names and fix it first, or fix the `.asd` (lisp-project skill).

#### Stage `compile`

The file reads, and `lisp-check` compiled it. Every compiler warning is a
problem, including a style warning.

```
src/math.lisp:5: compile: style-warning: Variable B is never used.
src/math.lisp:12: compile: warning: CAR should be given exactly 1 argument.  It was given 2 arguments.
src/math.lisp:20: compile: Package "UTILS" not found.
FAIL
```

`LINE` is where the **top-level form** containing the problem starts, usually
a `defun`. Search that whole form for the name in the message, and fix the
cause in the code so the warning goes away. Fixes for common warnings:
[references/compile-warnings.md](references/compile-warnings.md).

#### Stage `test` (only with `--test`)

The file compiled, and loading it ran the assertions. `tester` prints a
`Test failed:` block for each failed assertion, before the `test:` line:

```
Test failed: (ADD1 1)
  wanted: 5
     got: 2
src/math-tests.lisp:?: test: 1 of 4 assertions failed
FAIL
```

Fix the first `Test failed:` block. Change the code under test so the form
returns the wanted value; change the assertion only when its wanted value is
wrong. For other `test` messages, see
[references/tester-tests.md](references/tester-tests.md).

#### Lines that start with `lisp-check:`

```
lisp-check: Lisp binary 'alisp' not found. Install Allegro CL or set LISP_BIN to its path.
FAIL
```

A line that starts with `lisp-check:` is about the check itself, not your
file (exit code `2`). Leave the Lisp file as it is. Fix the command, or tell
the user what the message says and stop.

### Running lisp-check

```sh
lisp-check path/to/file.lisp
lisp-check --test path/to/file-tests.lisp
```

- Check one file per command.
- `lisp-check` runs Allegro CL in batch mode. It uses the binary named in the
  `LISP_BIN` environment variable, or `alisp` when `LISP_BIN` is not set:
  `LISP_BIN=/path/to/alisp lisp-check file.lisp`
- If the shell says `lisp-check: command not found`, run the `bin/lisp-check`
  script from the lisp-skills plugin by its full path. In Claude Code that is
  `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/bin/lisp-check`.

### Fixing compile warnings

Fix the first warning in the `lisp-check` output:

- `Variable B is never used`: remove `B`, use it, or add
  `(declare (ignore b))` when the argument must stay.
- `Free reference to undeclared variable *X*`: define `*X*` with
  `defvar` or `defparameter` above its first use, or fix the misspelled name.
- `undefined functions were referenced: F`: define `F`, fix the misspelled
  name, or add the package prefix.
- Wrong number of arguments: match the call to the function's lambda list.
- `Package "P" not found`: fix the package name, or define the package
  with `defpackage` before the code that uses it.

Fix the cause in the code so the warning goes away. The one declaration that
counts as a fix is `(declare (ignore ...))` for an argument the function must
accept but does not use.

### Tests for `lisp-check --test`

`lisp-check --test` loads the compiled file, and loading runs every top-level
`tester` assertion in it. Write test files in the shape of
`examples/count-words-tests.lisp`, which passes `lisp-check --test`. It starts:

```lisp
(eval-when (:compile-toplevel :load-toplevel :execute)
  (require :tester))

(defpackage :count-words-tests
  (:use :cl :util.test))

(in-package :count-words-tests)
```

then defines `count-words` and `first-word`, and ends with the assertions:

```lisp
(test 0 (count-words ""))
(test 3 (count-words "  read  compile test "))
(test '(0 1 2) (mapcar #'count-words '("" "lisp" "a b")) :test #'equal)
(test "read" (first-word "  read compile") :test #'string=)
(test-error (first-word "   "))
```

- Name the file `NAME-tests.lisp`.
- Start with the `eval-when` / `require` form, so the `util.test` package
  exists when the file compiles.
- Put each assertion at top level. `lisp-check` counts top-level assertions
  only; assertions inside `with-tests` give `no tester assertions ran`.
- `(test WANTED FORM)` compares with `eql`. Compare strings with
  `:test #'string=` and lists with `:test #'equal`.
- `test` fails with `additional value were returned from test form` when
  FORM returns more than one value, as `gethash`, `parse-integer` and
  `read-line` do. Keep only the first value:
  `(test 2 (values (gethash "and" *counts*)))`.
- A tests file for a project uses the project's package:
  `(:use :cl :util.test :tally)`. `lisp-check` loads the project's `.asd`
  first (lisp-project skill).
- `(test-error FORM)` passes when FORM signals a `simple-error`, which
  `(error "...")` does. For another condition class add
  `:condition-type 'CLASS`. Test errors your code signals itself: compiled
  code may skip type checks, so `(car 1)` can return garbage instead of
  signalling `type-error`.

#### Test output

```
 * * * UNEXPECTED TEST FAILURE * * *
Test failed: (ADD1 1)
  wanted: 5
     got: 2
src/math-tests.lisp:?: test: 1 of 2 assertions failed
FAIL
```

`tester` prints a block for each failed assertion: the form it ran, the value
wanted and the value it got. A `test-error` block says
`Reason: expected but did not detect an error`.

Other `test` messages:

- `error while running the tests: MESSAGE`: a top-level form signalled an
  error, so the assertions after it did not run. Fix that error first.
- `no tester assertions ran`: the file has no top-level assertions. Add
  them, or check the file without `--test` if it is not a test file.

## lisp-writing

Rules for writing Common Lisp for Allegro CL. Use when writing or editing Lisp code (.lisp, .cl), before running lisp-check.

Write Common Lisp the way a Lisp developer would. Follow every rule below.
Then check each file with `lisp-check` (the lisp-verify skill).

### Portable ANSI first

- Write portable ANSI Common Lisp. Use only the `cl` package by default.
- Use an Allegro extension (`excl:`, `excl.osi:`, `sys:`) only when ANSI
  has no way to do the job, for example running a shell command.
  Then read `references/allegro.md`.
- Load Allegro modules with `require`, for example `(require :osi)`.
  Assume no Quicklisp and no network.

### Common Lisp, not Scheme or Clojure

| Instead of             | Write                                        |
|------------------------|----------------------------------------------|
| `(define (f x) ...)`   | `(defun f (x) ...)`                          |
| `(define x 1)`         | `(defparameter *x* 1)` or `(let ((x 1)) ...)`|
| `(defn f [x] ...)`     | `(defun f (x) ...)`                          |
| `(fn [x] ...)`         | `(lambda (x) ...)`                           |
| `#t` / `#f`            | `t` / `nil`                                  |
| `'()` and `#f` as two values | `nil`: the empty list is false |
| `null?`, `pair?`       | `null`, `consp`                              |
| `set!`                 | `setf`                                       |
| `(f x)` where `f` is a variable holding a function | `(funcall f x)` |
| `begin`, Clojure `do`  | `progn`                                      |
| `cond` with `else`     | `cond` with `(t ...)` as the last clause     |
| `[1 2 3]`, `{:a 1}`    | `(list 1 2 3)`, a hash table                 |
| `"\n"`                 | `~%` inside `format` (`"\n"` is just `"n"`) |
| recursion for every loop | `loop`, `dolist`, `dotimes`                |

- Predicates end in `p`: `evenp`, `has-items-p`. Not `?`.
- `(first '())` and `(rest '())` return `nil`. They do not signal an error.
- A function and a variable can have the same name. Pass a function with
  `#'name`, call a function held in a variable with `funcall` or `apply`.

### Variables

- Global variables have earmuffs: `*name*`. Constants: `+name+` with `defconstant`.
- `defparameter` sets the value every time the file loads. Use it for
  settings you may change and reload.
- `defvar` sets the value only if the variable has none yet. Use it for state
  that must survive a reload, such as a cache or a counter.
- Define every global with `defvar` or `defparameter` before its first use.
  Plain `(setf *x* 1)` on an undefined variable is a compiler warning.
- Local variables: `let` binds all at once, `let*` binds in order, so a later
  binding can use an earlier one.
- Change a place with `setf`, `incf`, `decf`, `push`, `pop`.

### Equality

| Compare                         | Use                           |
|---------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| symbols, the same object        | `eq`                          |
| numbers of the same type, characters | `eql` (the default test) |
| numbers by value (`1` and `1.0`)| `=`                           |
| strings, case-sensitive         | `string=`                     |
| strings, case-insensitive       | `string-equal`                |
| lists, conses, strings          | `equal`                       |
| anything, ignoring case and number type | `equalp`              |

- `member`, `assoc`, `find`, `position`, `remove` and `gethash` use `eql` by
  default. `eql` is false for two strings with the same text. Pass
  `:test #'string=` or `:test #'equal` for strings and lists.
- A hash table with string keys needs `(make-hash-table :test #'equal)`.
- `gethash` returns two values: the value and whether the key was found.

### Case mode: alisp and mlisp

- `alisp` is ANSI mode, the default here. The reader turns symbol names to
  upper case: `foo`, `Foo` and `FOO` are the same symbol, named `"FOO"`.
- `mlisp` is case-sensitive: `foo` and `FOO` are different symbols, and
  `foo` is named `"foo"`. (Allegro Express ships only `alisp`, so `mlisp`
  behaviour is not verified here.)
- Write all code in lower case. Then it works in both modes.
- Never write a symbol name as a string. Make the name from a symbol:
  `(string '#:red)`, `(symbol-name 'red)`. In `defpackage`, write names as
  `#:name` or `:name`, not `"NAME"`.
- `(intern "foo")` and `(find-symbol "foo")` find a different symbol than
  `'foo` in `alisp`.

### More traps

- `sort` and `nreverse` destroy their argument. Sort a copy:
  `(sort (copy-list items) #'<)`. Never change a quoted literal like `'(3 1 2)`.
- Many functions return more than one value: `parse-integer`, `gethash`,
  `read-line`, `floor`. Wrap the call in `values` to keep only the first.
- `parse-integer` signals `parse-error` for bad input. Catch it with
  `handler-case` or pass `:junk-allowed t`.
- Use `cond` for more than two branches, `when`/`unless` for one branch.
  `if` takes exactly one then-form and one else-form; use `progn` for more.
- Keep a function short and give it a docstring.
- Unused argument: `(declare (ignore x))` as the first form of the body.

### Packages

Start each file with its package (from `examples/greeting.lisp`):

```lisp
(defpackage :greeting
  (:use :cl)
  (:export #:greet))

(in-package :greeting)

(defparameter *greeting* "Hello"
  "The word GREET puts before the name.")

(defun greet (name)
  "Return a greeting for NAME, for example \"Hello, Ada!\"."
  (format nil "~a, ~a!" *greeting* name))
```

For systems, ASDF and tests, use the lisp-project skill.

### References

Open a reference when you write that kind of code:

- `references/loop.md`: `loop` clauses (collect, sum, across, hash tables, return).
- `references/format.md`: `format` directives (`~a`, `~d`, `~%`, `~{~}`, padding).
- `references/clos.md`: `defclass`, `defgeneric`, `defmethod`, `print-object`.
- `references/conditions.md`: `handler-case`, `define-condition`, restarts,
  `unwind-protect`.
- `references/allegro.md`: shell commands, `excl:` string and regexp utilities,
  environment variables, case mode.

Every example in the references comes from a file in `examples/` that passes
`lisp-check --test`. `examples/traps-tests.lisp` shows each trap above.

### `loop` cheat-sheet

Each pattern is from `examples/loop-tests.lisp`, which passes `lisp-check --test`.

```lisp
;; Walk a list, build a new list.
(loop for n in numbers
      collect (* n n))                 ; (1 2 3) => (1 4 9)

;; Count from 1 to limit, including limit. Add up.
(loop for i from 1 to limit
      sum i)                           ; limit 3 => 6

;; Count from 0 up to n - 1.
(loop for i from 0 below (length sequence)
      collect i)                       ; "abc" => (0 1 2)

;; Filter.
(loop for n in numbers
      when (evenp n) collect n)        ; (1 2 3 4) => (2 4)

;; Walk a string or vector with ACROSS (IN is for lists only).
(loop for c across string
      count (char= c char))            ; #\a in "banana" => 3

;; Largest value. MINIMIZE for the smallest.
(loop for n in numbers
      maximize n)

;; Two FOR clauses step together and stop at the shorter list.
(loop for k in keys
      for v in values
      collect (cons k v))              ; (a b) (1 2) => ((a . 1) (b . 2))

;; Hash table keys. Use HASH-VALUES for the values.
(loop for k being the hash-keys of table
      collect k)

;; Leave early with a value. Without RETURN this loop returns NIL.
(loop for n in numbers
      for i from 0
      when (minusp n) do (return i))   ; (4 0 -1 -5) => 2

;; Stop with UNTIL or WHILE. FINALLY runs once at the end.
(loop for line in lines
      until (string= line "")
      do (incf count)
      finally (return count))
```

- `in` walks a list, `across` walks a vector or string, `on` walks the
  conses of a list.
- `to` includes the end, `below` stops one before it.
